paragraphs.heading: Why pantheism matters
paragraphs.edited: If naturalism is the dominant view of the West, pantheism is the dominant view of the East. Pantheism is interesting, and it may seem like much of pantheistic thought is far from your students. Even though it largely dominates Eastern culture, from Hindus to Buddhists and a bunch of others in that part of the world, it has made its way to the West — and in a really strange way. So you might think, for your youth group: why are we talking about pantheism? Why are we bothering with this? That's another part of the world, and I'm not taking my kids on a mission trip over there, so do I really need to spend an entire week dedicated to this sort of Eastern thought?

paragraphs.heading: The key idea of distinction
paragraphs.edited: So God is present everywhere. It defines life now, it defines life later, it defines relationships, it defines everything — how we see and relate to God. But the key I want you to get here is the idea of distinction, and this is going to be important as you move forward. If naturalism is saying there's no God at all, pantheism is saying, well, there is God, but God is not distinct from anything that's created. God is a part of creation, He's a part of you and me; there's just no distinction. There's no God and us. There's just everything all together. So for pantheism, there is no distinction at all. Keep that in the back of your mind, especially as we move to next week when we talk about monotheism. That's going to be really, really important.

paragraphs.heading: Paul at the Areopagus
paragraphs.edited: In our Bible study portion, we talk about Paul. We talk about Paul's interaction at the Areopagus on Mars Hill, and we talk about his interaction between the Epicureans and the Stoics. What's interesting is that these Stoics actually believed much of the same kinds of things that modern-day pantheism believes — that idea that God is somehow packed into every little piece of our world. And what Paul does is help them see that there is a distinction between the two: that God is here and we are here. That there's a separation. That although He's personal, although He's right here with us, He's distinct and other than us. And that's incredibly important.

paragraphs.heading: Speak truth in love
paragraphs.edited: Now, one quick word of note here that I want to make sure we're clear on. If you're doing everything really, really well, chances are you have some students who are either seeking or maybe skeptical, who have some questions and are curious. And as we're talking about other worldviews — whether they believe these things specifically or not — you want to be careful that we don't offend. We want to be careful that we speak truth, that we do so in love, but that we help them understand that these things are terribly inconsistent and they don't work.

paragraphs.heading: Remember this
paragraphs.edited: So remember: pantheism says God is all. God is in everything and a part of everything — the rocks, the trees, everything — and it's a divine force. And essentially, the key word here is that there is no distinction between God and creation, between creator and creation. Not only does this lead to the idea of idolatry — if we don't have the distinction, what does that make God? The very fact that we call Him God means that He is completely distinct, completely other than us, and completely holy.

paragraphs.edited: And the idea is this: if God is here and completely other than me, then I have a standard to look to, so I understand what's right and what's wrong. I understand what's just and unjust. I understand the idea of love versus hate. Putting God outside of myself and making God completely distinct helps us navigate reality in a way that makes sense. We have to have some kind of distinction. It's God who is other than, God who is holy, God who is supreme creator over all. And it's in Him that we live and move and have our being.
